extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature; literary critics; general educated readers interested in criticism and cultural analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual criteria for producing and evaluating literary criticism and for analyzing cultural representations of sex/gender and 'human-ness.' Emphasizes motives of criticism and threefold criteria for what counts as human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal-opinion criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The earliest and commonest is the mere expression of personal opinion, as is heard where young persons are becoming acquainted, the voluble 'I like this!' and 'Don't you like that?' and 'Isn't such a thing horrid?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of criticism has its value: it serves to show, even relentlessly to expose, the qualities and deficiencies of the critic—what one 'likes' merely shows what one is like. Anti-pattern: relying solely on personal liking is limited; vitality dies out when likings change and few people are interested in an inventory of limitations. Avoid making criticism only an inventory of tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority-motivated criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Another painfully common source of criticism--the desire to exhibit superiority. The aged, the elect, the conservative, and sometimes the professional critic criticize to prove their own superiority or to show that the general public is not 'as they are.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motive is a fault: critics who distrust warm approval or who condemn novelty chiefly to display superiority produce biased, unhelpful criticism. Anti-pattern: using criticism chiefly as social posturing or reputation-building; avoid letting elitist impulses determine judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional/pedagogic criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of criticism born of parental instinct, fostered by pedagogy: the desire to instruct and assist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a constructive and legitimate motive for criticism (positive alternative to mere opinion or superiority). Use criticism to guide, teach, and improve work; frame comments with the aim of helping authors or readers understand and grow. (Note: the page begins discussion of this motive but is cut off before full elaboration.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold criteria for human-ness
rubrics_metrics.description: Our human-ness is seen most clearly in three main lines: it is mechanical, psychical and social.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three dimensions to evaluate 'human-ness' in cultures, works, or characters: mechanical = power to make and use tools (tool-usage, craftsmanship, artifacts); psychical = degree of mental development (intelligence, counting, conceptual thought); social = mutual aid and the complexity of social relations (cooperation, division of labor, trade). These serve as substantive axes for analysis rather than sex-based explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish masculine, feminine, and human traits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three distinct fields of life--masculine, feminine and human. That is masculine which belongs to the male; that is feminine which belongs to the female; that is human which belongs to both alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing behavior, institutions, or literature, separate traits that are sex-specific from those that are human. Avoid conflating 'human' standards with male characteristics (the androcentric default). Apply this classification to expose misattribution (e.g., calling a woman's excellence 'masculine') and to identify where cultural labeling distorts understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for identifying androcentric culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Our historic period has been an Androcentric Culture: the history, the mental, the mechanical, the social development was almost wholly theirs; the world was taken for granted as 'his' world and women's roles sharply delimited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultures, institutions, and texts by asking whether human activities are monopolized by one sex and labeled 'man's work.' Look for signs such as: women set apart as 'the sex,' human standards based on male traits, language and naming that treats male as the human default, and institutional exclusion of women from the common human sphere. Use this criterion to critique gendered assumptions and to argue for reclassifying activities into the common human sphere.
